solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d is deceptive because students who know Guwahati changed hands multiple times may accept the generalised description but miss the incorrect attribution of it ever being under Maratha control.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (b): The Ahom capital was Garhgaon/Rangpur, not Guwahati — geographic precision is required; 'capital' is a false attribute for Guwahati.
Eliminate option (c): The Kamakhya temple is in Guwahati on Nilachal Hill, not in a different city — this is a geographic-swap attempt; Guwahati's religious significance is tied to Kamakhya.
Eliminate option (d): Guwahati was contested by Koch kingdom, Mughals, and Ahoms — Marathas did not contest Guwahati; this is a geographic-swap inserting the Marathas into northeastern history.

Confirm option (a): Guwahati's position as a Brahmaputra crossing point, confluence of trade routes, and gateway to the Assam heartland — explaining why Koch, Mughal, and Ahom powers all contested it — is the correct strategic characterisation.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (d) inserts the Marathas into the northeastern contest — a geographic-swap trap designed for students who know Guwahati 'changed hands multiple times' but cannot recall which specific powers contested it. The Marathas operated far to the south and west; they had no significant role in the Guwahati/Kamrup contest, which involved the Koch kingdom, Mughals, and Ahoms.
solution.final_explanation:
Guwahati's repeated contestation by multiple powers reflects its exceptional strategic geography in northeastern India.

• Option (a): Correct. Guwahati commanded the Brahmaputra's most important crossing point, sat at the convergence of trade routes, and controlled access to the Assam heartland. This explains why the Koch kingdom, Mughal empire, and Ahom kingdom all invested military resources in controlling it.
• Option (b): Incorrect. Guwahati was never the Ahom capital — that distinction belongs to Garhgaon (later Rangpur/Sibasagar area). This is the most frequent geographic confusion UPSC tests on this topic.
• Option (c): Incorrect. The Kamakhya temple IS located in Guwahati on Nilachal Hill — not in a different Assamese city. This option attempts a geographic-swap on the temple's location.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The powers that contested Guwahati were the Koch kingdom, the Mughal empire, and the Ahom kingdom — not the Marathas, who had no presence in the northeast.

Value Addition:
• The Koch kingdom (Koch Bihar and Koch Hajo) was the power immediately preceding Mughal occupation of Guwahati — they requested Mughal help against the Ahoms, which drew Mughal forces into the northeast.
• Guwahati's trade route significance stems from its position where the Brahmaputra narrows, making it the natural crossing point for movement between Bengal and upper Assam.
• The Kamakhya Devalaya (temple complex) makes Guwahati a pilgrimage destination to this day — adding cultural capital to its military-strategic value.

statement_analysis.reason: Momai Tamuli Borbarua, Lachit's father, was the first Borbarua of the Ahom kingdom — giving the family a documented place in Ahom administrative history.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (1 only is NOT correct) attracts students who incorrectly doubt the accuracy of Lachit's appointment by Chakradhwaj Singha, when that is in fact a correct statement.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Chakradhwaj Singha appointing Lachit as Borphukan for western Assam defense — correct; not a candidate for 'NOT correct.'
Evaluate Statement 2: Chakradhwaj Singha died in 1670 — Udayaditya Singha was the king at Saraighat (1671); this is NOT correct as stated.
Evaluate Statement 3: Momai Tamuli Borbarua as Lachit's father and first Borbarua — correct; not a candidate for 'NOT correct.'
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct — the answer is (d): 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 directly targets the most frequent misconception about the Battle of Saraighat: students associate Chakradhwaj Singha so strongly with the resistance (because he initiated it, appointed Lachit, and made the famous vow) that they forget he died in 1670 — a year before the battle. This entity-swap (Chakradhwaj for Udayaditya) is the most commonly tested trap in this topic.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ahom military-political leadership during the resistance to Mughal expansion requires precise attribution of roles to the correct kings.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Chakradhwaj Singha did appoint Lachit as Borphukan for the western Assam/Guwahati frontier — this is documented and accurate.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Chakradhwaj Singha died in 1670 — a year before Saraighat. The Battle of Saraighat (1671) was fought under his successor, Swargadeo Udayaditya Singha. The association of Chakradhwaj with Saraighat is one of the most common errors in this topic.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Momai Tamuli Borbarua (not Borphukan) was Lachit's father and the first holder of the Borbarua title in the Ahom kingdom — giving Lachit hereditary administrative standing.

Value Addition:
• The distinction between Borbarua (Lachit's father's title) and Borphukan (Lachit's own title) is a frequent UPSC trap on title confusion.
• Chakradhwaj Singha's death before Saraighat means the battle was fought without its principal political architect — Lachit essentially carried the mission forward under a new king.
• Udayaditya Singha's brief reign (1670–72) is historically significant precisely because it brackets the Battle of Saraighat — the victory belongs to his reign, even though the preparation was Chakradhwaj's.

Match B (Paik): Paik is the able-bodied male with corvée-military obligation — match with 4 (commoner male obligated to render military and labour service).
Match C (Garhgaon): Garhgaon was the Ahom capital, not Guwahati — match with 1 (the Ahom capital city, east of Guwahati).
Match D (Kamakhya): Kamakhya is the Shakti peetha temple in Guwahati whose protection motivated Ahom defense — match with 3 (major Shakti peetha in Guwahati whose protection motivated Ahom forces).
Correct combination: A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3 — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The critical trap is the Garhgaon–Guwahati confusion (C-1 vs. C-3). Students who know Guwahati is the more famous medieval Ahom-related city may place Garhgaon as the Kamakhya location (option c), not knowing that Kamakhya is specifically in Guwahati and Garhgaon is the actual Ahom capital. The two cities serve completely different roles in Ahom history, and conflating them is the exam trap.
solution.final_explanation:
Four key terms from Ahom history and geography require precise matching.

Correct matches:
• A (Buranji) — 2: Buranjis are the unique genre of Ahom/Assamese historical chronicles — the primary indigenous source for Ahom political and military history.
• B (Paik) — 4: A Paik is an able-bodied male commoner obligated to render military and labour service — the structural unit of Ahom military mobilisation.
• C (Garhgaon) — 1: Garhgaon (near modern Sibasagar) was the Ahom capital for most of the kingdom's history — east of Guwahati and distinct from it.
• D (Kamakhya) — 3: The Kamakhya temple on Nilachal Hill in Guwahati is one of the most important Shakti peethas in India, whose protection added religious motivation to Ahom defense of the city.

Trap pairing: C (Garhgaon) and D (Kamakhya) are the critical pair — students who conflate Guwahati's importance with the Ahom capital will place Garhgaon incorrectly.

Value Addition:
• The Tungkhungia Buranji is the most important Buranji for the Saraighat period — a specific text within the broader Buranji genre.
• Garhgaon's name means 'the capital village' in Assamese — a direct linguistic marker of its status as the seat of Ahom power.
• The Khel system organised Paiks into groups under Phukans — Khel is the intermediate organisational level between individual Paik and the Phukan commander.
